rationale_evidence.statement: Poses 4 mathematically coherent but mutually exclusive candidate ontologies for the carrier of K (Knowledge-as-primitive-object, risking circularity; Knowledge-as-structured-configuration over (objects,relations,qualifications,history), risking unproven reinvention of an earlier kernel; Knowledge-as-typed-graph, conflating representability with ontological necessity; Knowledge-as-opaque-algebraic-state, elegant for transitions but silent on the primitive-object question), none yet justified as canonical by the corpus.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Equality cannot be finalized before the ontology of K is fixed. This is a genuine dependency, not merely a missing glossary entry. ... T cannot be fully specified independently of K. This validates the dependency concern already identified in the earlier kernel analysis.
rationale_evidence.statement: Explains why equality and transition could not be finalized in earlier steps: both depend fundamentally on which of the 4 candidate ontologies (set/graph/provenance-sensitive/observational) is chosen for K -- set equality, graph isomorphism, provenance-equivalence, and behavioral equivalence are each appropriate under a different ontology, so neither equality nor transition can be specified independently of that prior choice, a genuine mathematical dependency rather than a glossary gap.

sources.note: Step 123's proposed KOS-SV-01 suite of seven test families (SV1 Provenance .. SV7 Feedback) mapped one-to-one onto the C1-C7 constitution, posed to test whether KnowledgeOS can produce machine-verifiable evidence that its own constitutional rules are currently satisfied.

rows.anchor: KOS-SV-01 ... SV1=Provenance ... SV7=Feedback.
rows.statement: Opens Step 123 (Self-Verification of KnowledgeOS): instead of manually applying the EEP to KnowledgeOS, defines how KnowledgeOS can verify its own constitutional invariants via a first self-verification suite KOS-SV-01 with seven test families mapped to the C1-C7 constitution (SV1 Provenance, SV2 Authority, SV3 EpistemicStatus, SV4 TemporalValidity, SV5 DeterministicAssurance, SV6 Traceability, SV7 Feedback); poses the decisive experiment 'can KnowledgeOS produce machine-verifiable evidence that its own constitutional rules are currently satisfied?' and states that a yes-answer crosses the boundary KnowledgeOS -> Self-Knowledge -> Self-Verification -> Self-Governance, framed as the foundation for KnowledgeOS as a self-assuring engineering system rather than merely a governed knowledge platform.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS → SelfObservation → SelfVerification
rows.statement: Reframes the question from 'can KnowledgeOS govern engineering?' to 'can KnowledgeOS prove that it itself conforms to the principles it imposes on engineering?' — the start of 'self-assuring architecture'; states the self-verification principle that the same Evidence Execution Protocol used on an engineering system (EEP(KnowledgeOS)) must be applicable to KnowledgeOS itself, making the platform both Subject and Verifier.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS → DeterministicChecks → Evidence → Verdict.
rows.statement: States the important boundary that self-verification does not mean KnowledgeOS declares itself correct (circular); it must instead run independently reproducible deterministic checks producing evidence and a verdict.

rows.anchor: SV-01 Provenance ... SV-07 Feedback
rows.statement: Restates KOS-SV as a table mapping SV-01..SV-07 one-to-one onto constitutional invariants C1-C7 (Provenance, Authority, Epistemic status, Temporal validity, Deterministic assurance, Traceability, Feedback).

rows.anchor: Q1 = {k | k.authoritative=True ∧ k.provenance=null}; |Q1|=0
rows.statement: SV-01 Provenance integrity test: query for authoritative knowledge objects with null provenance, expect zero results (else C1=FAIL); further distinguishes Valid(Provenance) from Present(Provenance) — e.g. source="unknown" is technically populated but semantically useless — and defines a five-level SV-01 assurance ladder: L1 field exists, L2 source identifiable, L3 origin process identifiable, L4 provenance immutable/auditable, L5 lineage traversable.

rows.anchor: Promotion(Proposed→Authoritative) with Authority=null → Reject
rows.statement: SV-02 Authority integrity: attempts promotion to authoritative status without valid authority, expecting rejection; introduces the negative-authorization-test principle — a positive test (authorized actors can approve) does not prove unauthorized actors cannot approve, so every governance control needs both a positive test (authorized_actor -> approve -> ALLOW) and a negative test (unauthorized_actor -> approve -> DENY); AuthorizationIntegrity = Positive + Negative.

rows.anchor: Inference → Authoritative without validation → DENY
rows.statement: SV-03 Epistemic integrity: attempting to promote an Inference directly to Authoritative without validation should DENY (worked as SV-03.1: Inference I-42 attempting status=Authoritative expects DENY); specifies the intended promotion pipeline Inference -> Candidate -> Evidence -> Verification -> Governance -> Authority -> Authoritative where no step should silently disappear; also flags the reverse failure mode 'epistemic downgrade' — a verified fact silently becoming an unsupported inference via a serialization/transformation error — requiring any Verified->Inferred transition to be explicit.

rows.anchor: K1 supersededBy K2; CurrentKnowledge = K2, not K1
rows.statement: SV-04 Temporal integrity: after K1 is superseded by K2, querying CurrentKnowledge must return K2 not K1; also requires preserving KnowledgeAt(t) for historical reconstruction (KnowledgeAt(2025) != CurrentKnowledge), worked as SV-04.1: D1 valid from January, D2 supersedes from June, Current(D)=D2 and At(March)=D1, expected PASS.

rows.anchor: V = f(Rule, Input, Version); V1 = V2
rows.statement: SV-05 Assurance integrity: a deterministic verification result V=f(Rule,Input,Version) run twice with identical inputs must reproduce (V1=V2; worked as SV-05.1: architecture-check --rule R17 run twice with same versioned inputs, expected PASS both times, else the verification mechanism itself needs investigation); requires a verification record to preserve RuleVersion, InputVersion, CheckerVersion, ExecutionContext for reproducibility.

rows.anchor: Action → Decision → Authority; untracked Action A82 → GovernanceFinding
rows.statement: SV-06 Traceability integrity: a positive test (Decision D42 -> Action A81) expects TraceExists=True; a negative test (untracked Action A82 with no decision) expects the system to actively recognize the missing relationship and raise a GovernanceFinding — stronger than merely failing a lookup query.

rows.anchor: Observation → Finding → Classification → Governance → Decision → Action → Verification → Updated Knowledge
rows.statement: SV-07 Feedback integrity, 'the most ambitious test': injects a synthetic ObservedDeviation and traces the full closed loop through six sub-tests (SV-07.1 Observation->FindingCreated; SV-07.2 Finding classified->GovernancePathAssigned; SV-07.3 Governance decision created (Finding->Decision); SV-07.4 remediation occurs (Decision->Action); SV-07.5 post-remediation observation matches expected, Finding->Verified->Closed; SV-07.6 knowledge state updates to contain the verified current state), assembled into one complete synthetic self-verification scenario diagram.

rows.anchor: SyntheticVerification ≠ UniversalCorrectness
rows.statement: Argues synthetic tests matter because historical production events may be incomplete, letting the suite deliberately exercise failure/authorization/correction/closure/feedback paths even without a historical incident (SyntheticEvidence can prove a mechanism exists); but limits this — synthetic verification proves the mechanism works under the tested scenario, not that every real-world scenario works (SyntheticVerification != UniversalCorrectness).

rows.anchor: TestID, Rule, Input, Expected, Actual, Evidence, Execution, Version, Timestamp, Verdict
rows.statement: Defines a self-verification result record schema (TestID/Rule/Input/Expected/Actual/Evidence/Execution/Version/Timestamp/Verdict) that itself becomes an evidence object; notes the recursive property that the SVResult is itself Evidence, so KnowledgeOS -> Evidence -> KnowledgeOS (the system records evidence about its own conformance).

rows.anchor: Verifier_A ≠ System_A
rows.statement: Warns that self-verification must not be the sole evidence of correctness (needs multiple layers: Static + Test + Runtime + IndependentReview) and states the independent-verifier principle: for high-value constitutional controls, the verifier should be a different system/process than the system under test (e.g. CI independently querying the DB for ProvenanceCompleteness) to reduce self-reporting risk.

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS API reports 'all authoritative decisions have provenance'; independent SQL check returns 17 records without provenance
rows.statement: Experiment: KnowledgeOS's own API claims full provenance coverage while an independent SQL check finds 17 records without provenance (APIClaim != Reality), verdict 'self-reporting failure' — presented as precisely why independent verification matters.

rows.anchor: S1 Self-reported ... S5 Independent governance review
rows.statement: Defines a five-level constitutional-evidence-tier hierarchy (S1 self-reported, S2 internal deterministic check, S3 external deterministic verifier, S4 runtime observation, S5 independent governance review), explicitly as a hierarchy of evidence strength rather than a requirement that every control reach S5.

rows.anchor: SV01 → Finding(C1Violation)
rows.statement: States a failed constitutional check should itself create a ConstitutionalFinding (e.g. SV01 -> Finding(C1Violation)) which then flows through the same governance loop, giving a recursive control cycle Constitution -> Check -> Finding -> Governance -> Remediation -> Check.

sources.note: Sixth and final governing verification directive in this batch, reframing the objective as finding the smallest set of unresolved decisions blocking theory completeness: mandates a 13-node true-blocking dependency chain with first-blocking-defect identification, a requirements-driven (not candidate-scoring) kernel derivation with a 5-way properties-of-state/relations/transformations/histories/actors separation, a 12-question adversarial attack on the verifier's own K={(q,s,e,c,t,u)} hypothesis, reframing epistemic status as a type-system problem (testing 5 candidate orthogonal status dimensions), explicit multi-notion equality/identity definitions revisited against 5 operations, a 5-class circularity classification, a fully-instantiated minimum executable kernel construction (no prose placeholders, no undefined oracles), a mathematical-validity/software-existence/empirical-correspondence three-way separated empirical boundary test, a causal (not chronological) blocking-lineage trace, a refined 5-value feedback-loop classification, a 12-point mathematical quality gate, a DDD/Ubiquitous-Language audit table over 16 terms, a ranked blocker list with 8-category classification, and a final 10-question decision tree with an explicit anti-editorial-reconciliation constraint list.

rows.anchor: Find the smallest set of unresolved mathematical, semantic and engineering decisions that prevents the KnowledgeOS theory from becoming a complete, computable and testable theory.
rows.statement: The directive reframes the objective from broad verification to finding the smallest set of unresolved decisions blocking theory completeness, explicitly instructing not to repeat the 9 already-established findings (competing kernel lineages, K undefined, equality unresolved, competing status vocabularies, circular definitions, undefined downstream operators, incomplete mathematical/engineering/empirical status, a confirmed mathematical error, the feedback-loop contamination risk) but to use them as the starting boundary.

rows.anchor: K -> equality/identity -> membership -> state construction -> state transition -> evidence/provenance semantics -> validation -> policy/governance -> replay -> decision operators -> measurement -> empirical validation -> KnowledgeOS implementation. ... Identify the first blocking defect in each depe
rows.statement: Mandates constructing a 13-node true-blocking dependency chain (K->equality/identity->membership->state construction->state transition->evidence/provenance semantics->validation->policy/governance->replay->decision operators->measurement->empirical validation->KnowledgeOS implementation), testing each node for definedness/typing/non-circularity/totality/determinism/computability/executability/testability/upstream-dependency, identifying the FIRST blocking defect in each chain rather than merely marking items missing.

rows.anchor: What must a knowledge state minimally contain in order for the claims made by the rest of the theory to be meaningful? ... properties of a state from relations between states from properties of transformations from properties of histories from properties of actors/policies/governance. Do not force e
rows.statement: Mandates deriving K's minimal content from REQUIREMENTS (13 named: proposition/assertion, epistemic status, evidence, provenance, context, temporal validity, uncertainty, contradiction, identity, missingness, supersession, lineage, transformation compatibility) rather than by scoring existing candidates, with a critical 5-way categorical separation (properties of a state / relations between states / properties of transformations / properties of histories / properties of actors-policies-governance) forbidding forcing everything into K.

rows.anchor: Treat it as a hypothesis, NOT as established theory. Try to refute it. ... Can it represent provenance without circularity? Attempt to construct counterexamples. If the model fails, repair it.
rows.statement: Mandates an adversarial 12-question refutation attack specifically on the verifier's own earlier K={(q,s,e,c,t,u)} recommendation, treating it strictly as an unproven hypothesis: testing each component's type/domain/primitiveness/comparability/instantiability/existence-without-transformation/unknown-expressiveness/contradiction-expressiveness/missingness-expressiveness/non-identifiability-expressiveness/circularity-free-provenance-representability, explicitly attempting counterexamples.

rows.anchor: truth status, evidence status, validation status, confidence, provenance status rather than one overloaded status field. Do not invent values merely to make the model work.
rows.statement: Reframes epistemic status resolution as a type-system problem rather than a mere crosswalk exercise: determining whether competing status vocabularies are synonyms, different abstraction levels, mutually exclusive states, orthogonal dimensions, historical vocabularies, or genuinely incompatible models, and specifically testing whether the theory needs separate orthogonal dimensions (truth status, evidence status, validation status, confidence, provenance status) rather than one overloaded status field -- forbidding inventing values merely to make the model work.

rows.anchor: structural equality, extensional equality, observational equality, cryptographic identity, semantic equivalence, or some combination. Then revisit: Replay, Merge, Supersede, Deduplicate, Contradiction detection using the actual equality definition.
rows.statement: Mandates explicitly defining 6 distinct equality/identity notions (structural, extensional, observational, cryptographic identity, semantic equivalence, or combinations) for knowledge states plus separately for proposition/evidence/transformation/state/version/provenance identity, then revisiting Replay/Merge/Supersede/Deduplicate/Contradiction-detection against the actual chosen equality definition, precisely recording any operation that cannot be defined due to inadequate equality.

rows.anchor: harmless mutual specification; recursive definition with valid base case; inductive definition; circular but repairable; logically invalid circularity. A recursive definition is not automatically circularity.
rows.statement: Mandates a circularity audit specifically targeting K/T/Policy/Evidence/Validation/Status/Identity/Lineage/Assessment/Governance for X-defined-using-Y-and-Y-defined-using-X patterns, classifying each cycle into 5 categories (harmless mutual specification, recursive definition with valid base case, inductive definition, circular-but-repairable, logically invalid circularity) -- a recursive definition is explicitly not automatically circularity if a base case or well-founded construction exists.

rows.anchor: one valid knowledge state can actually be constructed and transformed. ... K_0 then T(K_0,input,policy,context)->K_1 and calculate the result. Every symbol must have an explicit value. No prose placeholders. No 'assume an appropriate evaluator'.
rows.statement: Mandates constructing the minimum executable kernel: a fully concrete K_0, a fully concrete transformation T(K_0,input,policy,context)->K_1 with the result actually calculated -- every symbol must have an explicit value, forbidding prose placeholders, 'assume an appropriate evaluator' hand-waves, or undefined oracles unless the oracle is explicitly part of the model; if uncomputable, the exact blocker must be identified.

rows.anchor: mathematical validity from software existence from empirical correspondence. ... identify one real KnowledgeOS artifact; ... map it into the proposed mathematical representation; determine what cannot be represented. Do not call textual corpus analysis empirical evidence about KnowledgeOS.
rows.statement: Mandates a small reproducible empirical boundary probe performed only after the mathematical kernel is constructible: identify one real KnowledgeOS artifact, its metadata, transformation, and provenance, map it into the proposed representation, and determine what cannot be represented -- strictly separating mathematical validity from software existence from empirical correspondence, explicitly forbidding calling textual corpus analysis 'empirical evidence about KnowledgeOS'.

rows.anchor: first appearance -> later refinement -> contradiction -> latest formulation -> verification result -> current unresolved question. ... Why does this problem still exist after 240 steps? ... The purpose is causal reconstruction, not chronology for its own sake.
rows.statement: Mandates a targeted blocking-lineage trace (not a full historical re-review) for each unresolved blocker (K, transition, provenance, evidence, status, identity, policy, validation, measurement), answering why the problem still exists after 240 steps via a causal chain first-appearance->refinement->contradiction->latest-formulation->verification-result->current-unresolved-question -- explicitly causal reconstruction, not chronology for its own sake.

rows.anchor: SOURCE-INDEPENDENT; CORPUS DERIVED; VERIFIER-DERIVED; FEEDBACK-CONTAMINATED; INDEPENDENT CONVERGENCE. Never count verifier output echoed by the corpus as independent confirmation. However, do not treat feedback as useless. ... Did the corpus improve? Did the corpus independently prove the claim?
rows.statement: Refines the feedback-loop protection protocol into a 5-value classification (SOURCE-INDEPENDENT, CORPUS DERIVED, VERIFIER-DERIVED, FEEDBACK-CONTAMINATED, INDEPENDENT CONVERGENCE), explicitly noting feedback is not automatically useless -- it can be evidence the research process corrected itself -- but the two questions 'did the corpus improve' and 'did the corpus independently prove the claim' must be kept strictly separate.

rows.anchor: Type correctness ... Well-definedness ... Totality ... Determinism ... Closure ... Composition ... Identity ... Associativity ... Minimality: Do not claim minimality merely because a removal test did not find a failure in selected examples. Sufficiency: Do not infer sufficiency from minimality. Comp
rows.statement: The mathematical quality gate requires 12 explicit checks on every surviving central definition (type correctness, well-definedness, totality with boundary-case testing, determinism justification, closure, composition, identity, associativity before calling anything a semigroup/monoid, minimality -- explicitly not inferable merely from an incomplete removal test, sufficiency -- explicitly not inferable from minimality, computability with stated representation/input-size/algorithm/complexity, and 4 statistical-validity rules: no probability without a probability space/model, no estimator without an estimand, no confidence value without calibration semantics, no arithmetic on ordinal categories without justification).

rows.anchor: Term | Definition | Mathematical object | DDD object | Architectural object | Same meaning? ... overloaded terms; synonyms incorrectly treated as identical; one word representing multiple mathematical objects; ... The objective is a genuine Ubiquitous Language, not a glossary.
rows.statement: Mandates a DDD/Ubiquitous-Language audit over 16 named terms (Knowledge State, Evidence, Provenance, Transformation, Context, Validation, Assessment, Policy, Authority, Governance, Identity, Lineage, Status, Observation, Decision, Action) via a 6-column table (Definition, Mathematical object, DDD object, Architectural object, Same meaning?), flagging overloaded terms, false synonyms, one-word-multiple-objects, mathematical-objects-with-no-DDD-name, DDD-concepts-with-no-mathematical-semantics, and architecture-concepts-with-no-derivation -- the objective is a genuine Ubiquitous Language, not a glossary.

rows.anchor: BLOCKER 1 ... BLOCKER 2 ... DEFINITIONS; MATHEMATICAL PROOF; STATISTICAL MODEL; COMPUTABILITY; EMPIRICAL VALIDATION; DDD SEMANTICS; ARCHITECTURE; DOCUMENTATION. Do not call documentation a theory gap if the underlying mathematics is already established.
rows.statement: Mandates producing a ranked blocker list (BLOCKER 1 = smallest issue preventing formal completeness, BLOCKER 2 = next dependency, etc.), each classified into one of 8 categories (Definitions, Mathematical proof, Statistical model, Computability, Empirical validation, DDD semantics, Architecture, Documentation), explicitly forbidding mislabeling a documentation gap as a mathematical one or vice versa.

rows.anchor: A. Is the mathematical theory complete? ... F. Is the theory empirically validated against KnowledgeOS? YES/NO/PARTIAL ... I. What is the smallest remaining blocker? J. What exact experiment/proof resolves it?
rows.statement: The final decision tree requires exactly 10 explicit answers: (A) mathematical theory complete Y/N, (B) central K object formally defined Y/N, (C) computable Y/N/UNDER CONDITIONS, (D) at least one real state instantiated Y/N, (E) at least one real transformation executed Y/N, (F) empirically validated against KnowledgeOS Y/N/PARTIAL, (G) DDD Ubiquitous Language stable Y/N/PARTIAL, (H) architecture derivable from theory Y/N/PARTIAL, (I) the smallest remaining blocker, (J) the exact experiment/proof that resolves it.

rows.statement: States and sketches a proof for a Structural Completeness Theorem for R_req: R_req is structurally complete iff every minimal information requirement of every minimal operational task (contradiction isolation, Zero-state checking, epistemic query resolution, temporal garbage collection) maps to a non-collapsing partition. sources.note: Independently executed (exec/sigma.py) re-derivation of 272B's Sigma_min claims: Sigma0 = P({Support,Refute}) is confirmed a minimal 4-state space via pairwise-collapse deletion tests against corpus non-collapse laws (A1-A2); a NEW defect is found that Sigma0's derived 'Conflict' state is blind to the corpus's separate R_contradicts relation between two assertions (A3, two contradicting assertions both read 'Supported'); and OR-merge/Retract are proven jointly satisfiable only if Sigma is DERIVED from the evidence set rather than stored as a lattice element (A4), closing decision D-4 by derivation rather than by normative choice. Gamma is confirmed to belong outside Sigma (A5), and missingness is confirmed not representable by Sigma0 (A6, 'insufficient' collapses into 'Supported').

rows.statement: The regenerated transcript confirms exec/sigma.py's A1-A6 results were actually executed and produced the claimed output, serving as the evidentiary record for the whole Sigma-status package.

rows.anchor: NOTE: this is TRUE BY CONSTRUCTION once you posit exactly two independent predicates. The mathematical content is the CHOICE OF TWO, not the 4.
rows.statement: A1: the bijection Sigma0=P({Support,Refute}) ~= {0,1}^2 is confirmed (|P(S)|=4, states Unknown/Supported/Refuted/Conflict) but flagged as true by construction once exactly two independent predicates are posited -- the real mathematical content is the choice of Support/Refute as the two predicates, not the resulting count of four.

experiment.hypothesis: Sigma0, the powerset of {Support,Refute}, is isomorphic to {0,1}^2 and this fact is non-trivial
experiment.setup: direct powerset construction in Python
experiment.assumptions: exactly two independent evidence-polarity predicates, Support and Refute
experiment.method: enumerate the powerset and check bijection with {0,1}^2
experiment.result: bijection confirmed, but assessed as true by construction
experiment.interpretation: the substantive claim is which two predicates were chosen, not the resulting cardinality
experiment.limitations: none stated
experiment.conclusion: CONFIRMED, but a weaker result than it first appears

rows.anchor: collapse Unknown ~Refuted -> BREAKS: UNKNOWN != FALSE (42x) / Unknown != Absent (19x) ... => all 4 required. MINIMALITY CONFIRMED relative to these laws.
rows.statement: A2: each of the six pairwise collapses of the four Sigma0 states breaks a corpus-stated non-collapse law (e.g. UNKNOWN != FALSE 42x, empty != ContradictoryEvidence per S271.21, UNRESOLVED != INVALID 9x, insufficiency is not refutation), so minimality is confirmed relative to those specific laws -- a genuine deletion argument.

experiment.hypothesis: all four Sigma0 states are individually necessary
experiment.setup: six pairwise-collapse deletion tests against named corpus non-collapse laws
experiment.assumptions: the cited corpus laws are correctly quoted and still in force
experiment.method: for each pair, collapse and check whether a named law breaks
experiment.result: every one of six pairwise collapses breaks a distinct corpus law
experiment.interpretation: minimality holds relative to the tested laws, not as an absolute claim
experiment.limitations: minimality is conditioned on the specific laws tested, not proven unconditionally
experiment.conclusion: MINIMALITY CONFIRMED relative to tested laws

rows.anchor: Sigma0(c1)=Supported Sigma0(c2)=Supported <- both Supported, while (c1,c2,contradicts) holds. Sigma0 is BLIND to it, as (dir,str) was. *** THE REDUCTION DID NOT FIX THE Sigma-blind-to-R DEFECT. ***
rows.statement: A3: contradiction within a single assertion's evidence (Conflict={Support,Refute}) is derivable, but contradiction BETWEEN two assertions is a relation Sigma0 cannot express because Sigma0 is unary -- executed test constructs two assertions in an explicit contradicts-relation that both independently evaluate to Sigma0=Supported, proving the reduction to Sigma0 reproduces rather than fixes the earlier '(dir,str) blind to R' defect; a new finding not yet on any register.

experiment.hypothesis: Sigma0 can express contradiction between two assertions, not only within one assertion's evidence
experiment.setup: construct two assertions c1 ('tls=1.3') and c2 ('tls=1.2'), each with one supporting evidence item, joined by an explicit contradicts relation
experiment.assumptions: Sigma0 is computed per-assertion from that assertion's own evidence set
experiment.method: compute Sigma0(c1) and Sigma0(c2) independently and compare to the existence of the contradicts relation
experiment.result: Sigma0(c1)=Supported and Sigma0(c2)=Supported despite the contradicts relation holding
experiment.interpretation: Sigma0 is unary and blind to inter-assertion relational contradiction
experiment.limitations: none stated
experiment.conclusion: THE REDUCTION DID NOT FIX THE Sigma-blind-to-R DEFECT -- new finding, on no register

rows.anchor: union is a JOIN-semilattice op (monotone); retract is NON-monotone. They are compatible ONLY IF Sigma is DERIVED from the evidence set each time. ... OR-merge + retract TOGETHER FORCE Sigma to be DERIVED, not stored.
rows.statement: A4: OR-merge(Supported,Refuted)=Conflict is a monotone join-semilattice operation, but Retract (withdrawing the refuting item to recover Supported) requires subtraction and is non-monotone; the two are jointly satisfiable only if Sigma is recomputed (derived) from the evidence set on each query rather than stored as a lattice element -- a proof, not a normative choice, that Sigma must be DERIVED. This corrects the file author's own prior classification of decision D-4 as normative and closes D-4 by derivation.

lineage_claims.target: prior classification of D-4 as a normative decision
lineage_claims.quote: THIS IS A PROOF ABOUT D-4

experiment.hypothesis: OR-merge and Retract can both be supported by a Sigma value that is stored rather than recomputed
experiment.setup: symbolic construction: merge(Supported,Refuted); then retract the refuting evidence item
experiment.assumptions: merge is set union over evidence polarities; retract removes one evidence item
experiment.inputs: a Conflict state produced by merging Supported and Refuted
experiment.method: attempt to recover Supported from Conflict by removing the Refute polarity via set subtraction
experiment.result: subtraction recovers Supported only if Sigma is recomputed from the remaining evidence set; a stored lattice element carries no record of which evidence produced it
experiment.interpretation: OR-merge (monotone) and Retract (non-monotone) are jointly satisfiable only under a derived-Sigma design
experiment.limitations: none stated
experiment.conclusion: Sigma is DERIVED, not stored -- D-4 CLOSED by derivation

rows.anchor: Sigma0 has 4 states; a lossless single vocabulary needs >= 4*|Gamma|. => Gamma OUTSIDE Sigma. CONFIRMED, and 272B's Sigma _|_ Lambda _|_ Gamma agrees.
rows.statement: A5: ten constructed (Sigma,Gamma) cells are all independently meaningful, and the decisive corpus case S271.20 ('epistemically well-supported but administratively rejected') requires Gamma (governance) to sit outside Sigma (epistemic) since a lossless single vocabulary would need >= 4*|Gamma| values -- confirming Gamma's separation from Sigma, independently agreeing with 272B's Sigma-perp-Lambda-perp-Gamma orthogonality claim.

rows.anchor: MISSINGNESS IS NOT REPRESENTABLE BY Sigma0. It needs D_t + a sufficiency predicate. 272B does not claim otherwise -- but nor does it close it.
rows.statement: A6: Sigma0 maps three distinct epistemic situations ('never asked' has no Sigma value at all since no assertion exists; 'asked, no evidence' maps to Unknown; 'insufficient evidence' maps to Supported) onto only {undefined, Unknown, Supported} because Sigma0 has no sufficiency axis (Q was dropped from the ratified 6-tuple) -- missingness is not representable by Sigma0 and requires D_t plus a sufficiency predicate.

rows.statement: Sharp distinction: proving Sigma has a minimal four-valued semantic space is NOT the same as the full state representation being determined -- Sigma was only one of six blockers, closing it leaves five plus a newly discovered sixth (Sigma0-perp-R).

sources.note: A mandate requiring component-by-component adversarial attack on Step 245's K0 (pi, lambda, sigma, theta, C each tested against explicit alternative placements/models), a 10-row reconciliation table against prior findings, a theorem/counterexample discipline, and an 11-stage required derivation order (requirements->...->engineering validation) before any new kernel label may be proposed.

rows.anchor: What is the smallest formally valid mathematical system that can represent the KnowledgeOS semantics demonstrated by the corpus, without confusing state, evidence, assessment, transformation, governance and history? ... The final result may be: a Knowledge State, a state plus external assessment str
rows.statement: Reframes the central research question around minimality-without-confusion across 6 named categories (state, evidence, assessment, transformation, governance, history) and explicitly enumerates 5 possible final architectural shapes without pre-selecting any of them, forbidding K5/K8 selection as an answer.

rows.anchor: Given a concrete candidate K, can Claude actually calculate whether K in K? If not, K is still incompletely defined. ... Construct K_A, K_B [differing in evidence, epistemic qualification, temporal qualification, history]. ... T(K_A,input,context,policy,authority)=K_B ... No placeholders. No 'would'
rows.statement: Sets an operational completeness test for the validity predicate (can Claude actually compute K in K for a concrete candidate, not merely assert it), requires constructing two concrete states K_A/K_B differing along 4 axes (evidence, epistemic qualification, temporal qualification, history) rather than one, and requires an actually executed (not simulated or hedged with 'would') concrete transition with named/typed/valued arguments and an explicit precondition check before computing and validating the result.

rows.anchor: Do not force all operations to be transformations K->K. Validation may instead be K x X -> Assessment. Replay may be History x Input -> K. Authority may be Actor x Action x Context -> Authorization. Governance may be Policy x Transformation -> Assessment/Decision. These are hypotheses to test, not c
rows.statement: Rejects the assumption that every theory operation must have the shape K->K, proposing 4 differently-shaped candidate operation signatures (Validation: KxX->Assessment; Replay: History x Input -> K; Authority: Actor x Action x Context -> Authorization; Governance: Policy x Transformation -> Assessment/Decision), explicitly as hypotheses for the ten named operations (Add, Remove, Update, Merge, Supersede, Split, Accept, Reject, Validate, Replay), not settled conclusions.

rows.anchor: For every major proposed statement use: CLAIM, FORMALIZATION, ASSUMPTIONS, PROOF or COUNTEREXAMPLE, VERDICT. Never write 'therefore' unless the preceding reasoning actually establishes the implication.
rows.statement: Introduces a mandatory 5-part theorem/counterexample discipline (CLAIM / FORMALIZATION / ASSUMPTIONS / PROOF-or-COUNTEREXAMPLE / VERDICT) for every major statement in the deliverable, and an explicit ban on the connective 'therefore' unless the preceding reasoning actually establishes the implication -- a rhetorical-rigor constraint not present in the batch's earlier mandates.

rows.statement: Requires a 10-question engineering test mapping a real KnowledgeOS/EKS artifact onto the theory's categories (state, proposition, observation, evidence, assessment, transformation, policy, authority, lineage, resulting state), with any invented field recorded as an implementation gap rather than silently patched, and an explicit ban on adjusting the theory to accommodate one artifact.

rows.anchor: Model B executed -- K=(C,sigma,theta,lambda) with policy as an argument to T ... If pi in K, then revoking or amending a policy changes every stored state, while nothing that is known has changed. ... VERDICT: pi is EXTERNAL. MATHEMATICALLY VERIFIED by counterexample.
rows.statement: Executes Model B (policy external to K, passed as an argument to T) successfully, and gives a counterexample against Model A (policy internal): if pi were in K, revoking/amending a policy would change every stored state despite no change in what is known, and two states holding identical knowledge under different policies would be unequal -- policy governs the transition, not what is known. Verdict: pi is external to K, mathematically verified.

experiment.hypothesis: Policy pi is external to the Knowledge State, not a component of it.
experiment.setup: Model A (pi in K) vs Model B (pi as T argument).
experiment.assumptions: policy revocation should not retroactively alter recorded knowledge
experiment.method: execution of Model B; counterexample construction against Model A
experiment.result: Model B runs correctly with the state needing no policy field; Model A produces an absurd consequence (policy revocation changes stored states)
experiment.interpretation: pi belongs outside K
experiment.limitations: single worked example
experiment.conclusion: pi is EXTERNAL, mathematically verified

rows.anchor: same proposition, different evidence: Observed vs Supported ... same proposition+evidence, different policy: Observed vs Unknown ... Model 1 REFUTED ... Model 2 REFUTED (insufficient) ... Model 3 SURVIVES ... sigma is not a primitive of the Knowledge State. It is derived from an Assessment.
rows.statement: Tests all three S1602-mandated sigma models by execution: Model 1 (sigma:Proposition->Status) is refuted because one proposition yields three distinct status values depending on context; Model 2 (adding Evidence,Context) is refuted as insufficient because policy also changes the outcome and is not an argument; Model 3 (a full Assessment function over Proposition,Evidence,Context,Policy, with Status derived) survives. Concludes epistemic status is a derived Assessment output, not a Knowledge-State primitive -- noted as exactly Step 232.4's Validation:K x X->Assessment shape, extended to status, which Step 245 had re-internalized as a primitive.

rows.statement: Gives a direct counterexample refuting theta as a function of Proposition alone: the same proposition can carry two overlapping-but-distinct assertion instances with different validity intervals, which a single-valued function theta:Proposition->Interval cannot represent. Verdict: temporal validity belongs to the assertion instance, mathematically verified; also notes the four bitemporal dimensions (valid/known/record/decision time) are not collapsible to one timestamp, yet the real implementation does collapse them to a single decidedAt field -- flagged as an IMPLEMENTATION GAP.

sources.note: The 'Knowledge Calculus' computational-breakthrough proposal (S2295): natural-deduction-style inference rules, a rewriting-system/confluence hypothesis, and a four-level definition of 'computational'.

rows.anchor: The breakthrough would not be proving that the Gītā mathematically describes KnowledgeOS. It would be discovering that the philosophical model has led us to a new computational theory of evolving knowledge states with precise mathematics, executable operators, invariants, and measurable convergence. ... Yes, the theory should be computational -- but not necessarily reducible to computation.
rows.statement: Carefully defines what a genuine theoretical breakthrough would mean here: not proving the Gita mathematically describes KnowledgeOS, but discovering that the philosophical model led to a new computational theory of evolving knowledge states with precise mathematics, executable operators, invariants, and measurable convergence -- with the theory being computational but not necessarily reducible to computation.

rows.anchor: Level 1 -- Representational: can we represent K_t in a computer? Obviously yes. Level 2 -- Operational: can every operator be executed, O_i(K_t)->K_{t+1}? This is where KnowledgeOS becomes a real computational theory. Level 3 -- Verifiable: can we automatically check I(K_{t+1}) and reject invalid transformations? Level 4 -- Theoretical computation: can we characterize what the Kernel can and cannot compute -- termination, determinism, confluence, soundness, completeness, computational complexity, decidability? This would be genuine theoretical computer science.
rows.statement: Defines four increasingly demanding levels of 'computational': Level 1 Representational (K_t is representable, trivially true); Level 2 Operational (every operator is actually executable, O_i(K_t)->K_{t+1} -- where KnowledgeOS becomes a real computational theory); Level 3 Verifiable (invariants I(K_{t+1}) can be automatically checked, invalid transformations rejected); Level 4 Theoretical computation (proving termination, determinism, confluence, soundness, completeness, computational complexity, decidability -- 'genuine theoretical computer science').

rows.anchor: P(K_t|E_t). An observation E_{t+1} causes P(K_t|E_t) -> P(K_{t+1}|E_t,E_{t+1}). Now the Kernel can computationally perform: belief updating, uncertainty reduction, hypothesis comparison, anomaly detection, contradiction detection, evidence weighting. Measure H(K_t) using entropy. H(K_{t+1})<H(K_t). But lower uncertainty != necessarily more truth. A confidently wrong model has low uncertainty. So evidence validity remains essential.
rows.statement: Proposes a Bayesian/statistical layer: knowledge as P(K_t|E_t), updating on new evidence P(K_t|E_t)->P(K_{t+1}|E_t,E_{t+1}), enabling six computational operations (belief updating, uncertainty reduction, hypothesis comparison, anomaly detection, contradiction detection, evidence weighting), and an entropy measure H(K_t) with H(K_{t+1})<H(K_t) as a candidate improvement signal -- but explicitly warns lower uncertainty is not necessarily more truth (a confidently wrong model has low uncertainty), so evidence validity remains essential.

rows.anchor: Can a Knowledge State be transformed toward a formally defined epistemic optimum? K_0 -T1-> K_1 -T2-> K_2 -> ... -> K* where K* satisfies T(K*)=K* or P(K*)=max P(K). Then investigate whether K_t -> K* is guaranteed under certain conditions. That would be a serious mathematical result.
rows.statement: Poses the 'ultimate computational question': can a knowledge state be transformed toward a formally defined epistemic optimum K*, satisfying either a fixed-point condition T(K*)=K* or a maximality condition P(K*)=max P(K)? Investigating whether convergence K_t -> K* is guaranteed under certain conditions is named a potentially serious mathematical result.

rows.anchor: We must not make the mistake of defining KnowledgeOS = Truth Machine. No computational system can automatically guarantee truth about an arbitrary external reality. Fundamental limitations: incomplete observations, noisy measurements, undecidability, computational complexity, inconsistent evidence, model dependence, semantic ambiguity. A more defensible objective: KnowledgeOS computes justified transformations of represented knowledge, rather than KnowledgeOS computes truth.
rows.statement: States a fundamental limit guarding against overreach: KnowledgeOS must never be defined as a 'Truth Machine,' since no computational system can guarantee truth about arbitrary external reality, citing seven fundamental limitations (incomplete observations, noisy measurements, undecidability, computational complexity, inconsistent evidence, model dependence, semantic ambiguity). Proposes the more defensible objective: 'KnowledgeOS computes justified transformations of represented knowledge,' not 'KnowledgeOS computes truth.'

sources.note: S0522's extraction from Dretske: information ≠ meaning (Event/State->Information->Coding->Meaning->Belief->Knowledge); information as reduction of a possibility space; a channel/calibration distinction between knowledge-about-domain, knowledge-about-evidence-source, and knowledge-about-observation-mechanism-reliability; information-caused belief as an alternative to Floridi's relevance+account route to knowledge; nested informational shells reframing 'knowledge depth'; Information ≠ Belief ≠ Knowledge; and a representation-independence principle. Read explicitly in comparison with floridi-philosophy-of-information-lens (S0521), proposing a Floridi x Dretske comparative matrix as the next step.

rows.anchor: information is not the same thing as meaning. ... information can exist objectively in the relationships between events before interpretation, while meaning is something that develops through systems capable of exploiting that information. ... EVENT/STATE -> INFORMATION -> CODING/REPRESENTATION -> MEANING -> BELIEF -> KNOWLEDGE.
rows.statement: Reports Dretske's central distinction information != meaning (information exists objectively in relationships between events prior to interpretation; meaning develops through systems capable of exploiting it), formalized as Event/State->Information->Coding/Representation->Meaning->Belief->Knowledge, replacing a simpler word->meaning->knowledge chain.

rows.anchor: information as a reduction/elimination of possibilities. His simple example reduces eight possible candidates to one, producing 3 bits of information. ... POSSIBILITY SPACE -> [observation/signal] -> REDUCED POSSIBILITY SPACE -> INFORMATION. This is potentially more fundamental than our current concept of "knowledge item." ... A signal carries the information that s is F when, given the signal and relevant background knowledge, the conditional probability of s being F is 1, whereas given the background knowledge alone it is less than 1.
rows.statement: Reports Dretske's information-theoretic foundation treating information as reduction of a possibility space (eight candidates reduced to one yields 3 bits), proposed as potentially more fundamental than 'knowledge item'; formalizes his semantic-information definition: a signal carries the information that s is F when P(s is F | signal, background) = 1 while P(s is F | background alone) < 1, flagged as directly relevant to the project's truth/evidence/observation/assurance work.

type_signature.codomain: conditional probability of s being F

rows.anchor: the same amount of information can be represented by very different codes ... Words and sentences are representations. They are not the fundamental knowledge objects. Dretske gives us very strong support for that conclusion.
rows.statement: Reports Dretske's separation of information from the representation/code carrying it (the same information can be encoded longer/shorter/redundant), reinforcing the KNOWLEDGE DOMAIN (fact/proposition/information/evidence/relation) vs REPRESENTATION LAYER (words/sentences/documents/diagrams/code/embeddings) separation and the conclusion that words/sentences are representations, not fundamental knowledge objects.

rows.anchor: checking whether the instrument itself is reliable is a different informational operation. During calibration, the instrument temporarily becomes the object of investigation rather than simply the channel. ... knowledge about the domain; knowledge about the evidence source; knowledge about the reliability of the observation mechanism.
rows.statement: Uses Dretske's calibration example (a measuring instrument transmits information about a measured system, but checking the instrument's own reliability is a distinct informational operation where the instrument temporarily becomes the object of investigation) to derive three distinct knowledge types KnowledgeOS must separate: knowledge about the domain, knowledge about the evidence source, and knowledge about the reliability of the observation mechanism, with a parallel Channel->Calibration->Channel Reliability path alongside Source->Channel->Observation->Evidence->Information->Belief->Knowledge.

rows.anchor: Dretske instead develops: information -> information-caused belief -> knowledge. He explicitly proposes an information-theoretic replacement for the traditional justified-true-belief account. ... a particularly subtle distinction between information causing a belief and information causally sustaining a belief. ... OBSERVATION -> INFORMATION ACQUISITION -> BELIEF FORMATION -> BELIEF SUSTENANCE -> KNOWLEDGE CLAIM.
rows.statement: Contrasts Floridi's semantic-information->relevance->account->knowledge route with Dretske's information->information-caused-belief->knowledge route (an information-theoretic replacement for justified-true-belief), distinguishing information causing a belief from information causally sustaining it, proposing a five-stage pipeline Observation->Information Acquisition->Belief Formation->Belief Sustenance->Knowledge Claim instead of treating evidence as a static attachment to a claim.

rows.anchor: nested informational shells. A structure may carry information that t is a square while that information is nested inside information about another object, which may itself be nested inside something else. ... knowledge depth may not simply be graph distance. It may involve informational containment/specificity/dependency.
rows.statement: Reports Dretske's Chapter-7 'nested informational shells' (information about one thing can be nested inside information about another, recursively), proposing this refines the project's 'knowledge depth' problem: depth may not be graph distance but informational containment/specificity/dependency.

lineage_claims.quote: This is extraordinarily close to the thing we were trying to express when we talked about: going deeper and deeper through connected knowledge. But Dretske gives us a better conceptual vocabulary

rows.anchor: information carried by a semantic structure cannot be false, while beliefs can be false. Therefore: INFORMATION ≠ BELIEF ≠ KNOWLEDGE. ... Dretske explicitly distinguishes the concept from a particular belief: structure types have meaning, while tokens can have truth value.
rows.statement: Derives Information != Belief != Knowledge from Dretske's point that information (as he defines it) cannot be false while beliefs can, and separately distinguishes concept (a structure type, carrying meaning) from a particular belief (a token, carrying truth value) -- flagged as crucial for the Kernel.

rows.anchor: a system's semantic content can remain the same even when its physical realization differs; two physically different structures can have the same semantic content. ... KnowledgeOS should be representation-independent. The Kernel should not care whether knowledge is represented as JSON, SQL, Markdown, PDF, graph, vector, sentence, code, database record, AI context. What matters is the informational/semantic structure being represented.
rows.statement: Uses Dretske's multiple-realizability point (same semantic content, different physical realizations) to state a representation-independence principle: the Kernel must not care whether knowledge is represented as JSON/SQL/Markdown/PDF/graph/vector/sentence/code/database-record/AI-context -- only the informational/semantic structure matters.
invariants: Kernel behavior must not depend on physical representation format

rows.anchor: Floridi and Dretske are converging on some things but disagreeing or emphasizing different layers on others. That is precisely what we need from the Zero Lens. ... I would not freeze the Kernel yet. The next useful step is to construct a Floridi × Dretske comparative matrix and derive only the invariants that survive both books.
rows.statement: Notes Floridi and Dretske converge on some points and diverge/emphasize different layers on others, which is exactly the intended use of the Zero Lens; explicitly declines to freeze the Kernel, proposing a Floridi x Dretske comparative matrix to derive only the invariants surviving both books as the next research step.

sources.note: Step 69's execution-boundary layer: Architecture≠Algorithm, the T:S×E→S∪Error transition formalism, Computability≠Feasibility, symbolic-representation/solver-delegation for state-space explosion, the six-item EpistemicLimit taxonomy, agent-workflow termination/execution-budget controls, Sound-vs-Complete, the five-level assurance hierarchy, and the LocalFirst-DistributedWhenNecessary deployment principle culminating in the five-way Computable/Decidable/Identifiable/Feasible/EpistemicallyValid distinction. Substantially extends computational-realizability-principle (B0020) and kos-primitive-reduction-kernel's computability section (Step 49) with new experiments and taxonomy.

rows.anchor: Architecture != Algorithm; finite representation x∈Σ*; state transition T:S×E→S∪Error rejecting invariant violations
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS's architecture can specify semantic contracts (Knowledge, Evidence, Inference, Causality, Decision) without mandating one universal algorithm per operation -- Architecture != Algorithm, allowing multiple computational implementations. Requires every artifact to have a finite representation x in Sigma* (JSON, database records, graph nodes, event records, model metadata, hashes, identifiers). Formalizes S_{t+1}=T(S_t,e_t) as an executable event-transition chain, and strengthens T to T: S x E -> S union Error, rejecting an event when it would violate an invariant.

rows.anchor: Experiments 1-3: finite state transition, invalid-type-transition rejection, deterministic-bounds-checked probabilistic claim acceptance
rows.statement: Experiment 1: computing T(S0,e1) yields S1 as ordinary computation -- PASS. Experiment 2: attempting Prediction->VerifiedFact with no validation evidence yields T(S,e)=EpistemicTypeError -- PASS, illustrating that deterministic rule evaluation (if type(x)=Prediction and target=VerifiedFact and not-Validated then Reject) does not require an AI to 'understand' the rule -- 'exactly where deterministic assurance becomes powerful'. Separates deterministic computation f(x)=y from probabilistic computation P(Y|X): the deterministic layer verifies schema/type/provenance/authorization/invariant-satisfaction/graph-integrity/version-compatibility/cryptographic-integrity, while the AI/statistical layer performs inference/prediction/classification/hypothesis-generation/probabilistic-reasoning -- giving 'AI reasoning + Deterministic assurance'. Experiment 3: an AI output P(p)=0.82 checked deterministically for 0<=0.82<=1 plus ModelVersion/Provenance yields AcceptedAsProbabilisticClaim -- PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: State transitions correctly execute valid events, reject invariant-violating (type-unsafe) events, and correctly bounds-check probabilistic AI outputs deterministically.
experiment.setup: Three experiments (69.5, 69.8, 69.12).
experiment.assumptions: The type-system and invariant machinery from Steps 48/67 are assumed correctly specified.
experiment.inputs: Three scenario premises as summarized in the statement.
experiment.method: Compute the transition/check and compare against the expected result.
experiment.result: All three experiments PASS.
experiment.interpretation: Deterministic assurance and probabilistic AI output can be combined without either compromising the other.
experiment.limitations: Manual scenario reasoning, not an executed implementation.
experiment.conclusion: Experiments 1-3 PASS.

rows.anchor: Computability != Feasibility; deployment independence of semantic results; three computational classes
rows.statement: Distinguishes Class A Easy/ordinary (O(n), O(n log n)), Class B Expensive but computable (O(n^2), O(n^3), or exponential for modest n), Class C Not generally computable (no general algorithm) -- 'expensive is not the same as uncomputable'. States a problem may be Computable=True yet Practically Infeasible=True (e.g. requiring 10^100 operations) -- Computability != Feasibility. Experiment 5: a finite optimization problem whose exact solution requires enormous computation is Computable but PracticallyInfeasible -- PASS. Introduces a ComputationalProfile C=(Time,Memory,DataVolume,ModelSize,Parallelism) metadata concept, classifying operations as Local/Parallel/Distributed/ExternalService (e.g. TypeCheck/ProvenanceValidation/SmallGraphTraversal/RuleEvaluation locally; LLMInference/LargeEmbeddingGeneration/LargeSimulation on GPU/large machines; MassiveDataProcessing/LargeScaleModelTraining potentially distributed). States the architectural principle SemanticArchitecture should not depend on ComputationalDeployment: the same semantic operation may run locally or distributed. Experiment 6: validating I(x) on laptop/server/distributed worker yields SameSemanticResult given deterministic implementation and equivalent inputs -- PASS.
invariants: SemanticArchitecture does not depend on ComputationalDeployment

rows.anchor: State-space explosion avoided via symbolic representation and solver delegation; KnowledgeOS should not become a UniversalSolver
rows.statement: For n binary variables the state space is 2^n (e.g. ~1.27e30 for n=100), which cannot be enumerated -- but KnowledgeOS does not need to: it can represent CurrentState and Constraints symbolically (e.g. x1+x2<=1) and delegate to constraint solving/SAT-SMT/symbolic algebra/optimization engines. Experiment 7: attempting to enumerate 100 binary variables' full state space is ComputationallyInfeasible, but the symbolic representation remains manageable -- PASS. States the DDD conclusion: KnowledgeOS should not become a UniversalSolver; it defines the SemanticContract and delegates specialized computation. Experiment 8: KnowledgeOS creates a SolverRequest for an OptimizationProblem, receives a Solution from an external solver, and validates the result and provenance rather than implementing every optimizer internally -- PASS, giving a clean architecture (Rule Engine / Statistics / AI-ML feeding a Validated Result under KnowledgeOS governance).

lineage_claims.quote: KnowledgeOS should not become: UniversalSolver.

rows.anchor: Undecidability re-derived; undecidable-request refusal experiment; six-item EpistemicLimit taxonomy
rows.statement: Re-derives that a universal termination check (halting problem) is not computable, and that this does not invalidate KnowledgeOS: it must instead represent Unknown or UndecidableUnderCurrentModel. Experiment 9: asked to determine termination for every arbitrary program, the system correctly returns NoUniversalAlgorithm rather than fabricating an answer -- PASS. Consolidates a formal limitation taxonomy EpistemicLimit = {Unknown, Uncertain, Unobservable, NonIdentified, Infeasible, Undecidable}, each with different meanings and remedies. Experiment 10: constructing one example of each limitation, the system preserves their distinct semantic reasons rather than collapsing them into a generic 'error' -- PASS.

lineage_claims.target: kos-partial-observability-epistemic-boundary's five-state epistemic taxonomy (Step 66) and kos-causal-identifiability-invariants's NotIdentified (Step 63)
lineage_claims.quote: This reinforces Step 66... EpistemicLimit = {Unknown, Uncertain, Unobservable, NonIdentified, Infeasible, Undecidable}.

rows.anchor: Agent workflow termination controls: cycle detection and execution budgets (MaxSteps/MaxTime/MaxTokens/MaxCost/MaxDepth)
rows.statement: Warns an unbounded agent workflow (A->B->C->A) can loop forever, requiring termination controls. Experiment 11: A->B->A correctly yields CycleDetected or ExecutionBudgetExceeded -- PASS. Defines execution budget dimensions MaxSteps, MaxTime, MaxTokens, MaxCost, MaxDepth, making AI computation operationally controllable and runnable locally (e.g. MaxSteps=20 guarantees termination even on non-convergent reasoning). Experiment 12: an agent failing to converge after 20 iterations yields ReasoningTimeout rather than infinite execution -- PASS.

lineage_claims.quote: AgentWorkflow needs termination controls.

rows.anchor: Sound vs Complete distinction; soundness preferred for high-integrity subsystems; finite-test-extrapolation rejected
rows.statement: Distinguishes Sound (if the system derives p, p is valid under its rules) from Complete (if p is derivable under the rules, the system will find it) as different properties. States for high-integrity transformations FalsePositive may be more dangerous than FalseNegative, so some subsystems should prioritize Soundness. Experiment 13: a validator checking only known invariant violations (not proving no unknown issue exists) correctly yields ValidatedUnderRules rather than AbsolutelyCorrect -- PASS, giving the defensible statement 'the artifact satisfies the specified validation rules' rather than 'reality is correct'. Notes some components may be formally proved (for-all x in D: I(x)) while others can only be tested on finite examples (I(x_1),...,I(x_n)), which never establishes universal correctness. Experiment 14: 1,000 successful tests do not license an AI claiming SystemCorrectForAllInputs -- Rejected -- PASS.

rows.anchor: Five-level assurance hierarchy; assurance-inflation rejection experiment
rows.statement: Distinguishes a testing/verification hierarchy: ExampleTest, PropertyTest, InvariantTest, ModelCheck, FormalProof, each providing different assurance, and defines an AssuranceLevel taxonomy Observed / Tested / InvariantValidated / FormallyVerified -- 'not one universal truth score'. Experiment 15: a component passing only unit tests being labeled FormallyVerified is Rejected -- PASS, an 'assurance inflation' failure mode.

lineage_claims.quote: AssuranceLevel... Observed, Tested, InvariantValidated, FormallyVerified.

rows.anchor: Core computability theorem; five-way final distinction (Computable/Decidable/Identifiable/ComputationallyFeasible/EpistemicallyValid); LocalFirst-DistributedWhenNecessary
rows.statement: States the core computability theorem: KnowledgeOS core semantics are computable because its artifacts, states, transitions, and invariants can be represented finitely -- but not every question posed to it will be decidable, identifiable, or computationally feasible. Concludes a normal PC suffices for knowledge-graph operations, event processing, provenance, type checking, deterministic assurance, workflow orchestration, moderate statistical computation, local databases, and small/medium AI models; large-scale training/inference is a separate concern. States SemanticComplexity != HardwareRequirement -- hardware is determined by DataVolume, GraphSize, QueryRate, ModelSize, InferenceLatency, TrainingRequirement, Concurrency, not conceptual richness. Gives the principle LocalFirst, DistributedWhenNecessary: implement the Core on a developer workstation, benchmark it, and distribute only after observing actual bottlenecks. States the final five-way distinction that must never collapse: Computable, Decidable, Identifiable, ComputationallyFeasible, EpistemicallyValid.
invariants: Computable, Decidable, Identifiable, ComputationallyFeasible, and EpistemicallyValid are five distinct, non-collapsible dimensions

rows.statement: Proposes the file's most important improvement: separating operations into three distinct kinds rather than one operator catalogue -- (A) knowledge-state operations O_K: K->K' (Create, Revise, Retract, Supersede, Merge, Split, Qualify, none canonical), (B) epistemic-analysis operations O_E: (K,X)->Y which may inspect/evaluate without changing K (Compare, Classify, DetectContradiction, EvaluateEvidence, DetermineIdentity, CheckConsistency), and (C) world/action operations O_W: (K,D)->W' crossing the KnowledgeOS/world boundary (Authorize, Execute, Notify, Publish, Apply), which should become a formal boundary rather than an illustrative diagram only.

sources.note: A self-declared [RATIFIED] Contradiction Isolation & Resolution Semantics spec: Contr(p) iff S+(p)>0 and S-(p)>0 within a context, distinguished by threshold tau from Underdetermined (S+=S-=0) and Uncertain (small positive S+, S-=0); a five-type contradiction typology (Direct, Source, Rule, Observation, Interpretation) each with a formal triggering condition; a non-explosion postulate defining an isolation-scope closure Contr_scope(p) = {p} union Dependents(p) union ConflictingSources(p); a four-state lifecycle (DETECTED->ISOLATED->TRIAGED->RESOLVED); and four named resolution operators (Supersede, Contextualize, Retract, Discount) each with a formal signature and effect, plus a Python ContradictionEngine reference implementation.

rows.anchor: Contr(p) iff (S+(p)>0) and (S-(p)>0) within Context C ... Underdetermined: S+(p)=0 and S-(p)=0 (No evidence). Uncertain: S+(p)=epsilon and S-(p)=0 (Low confidence positive evidence). Contradiction (Contr): S+(p)>tau and S-(p)>tau (Sufficient conflicting evidence). Type(Contr) in {Direct, Source, Rule, Observation, Interpretation}
rows.statement: SPEC-CONTR-2026-v1.0 defines Contr(p) as sufficient conflicting evidence (S+(p)>tau and S-(p)>tau within a context), distinct from Underdetermined (S+=S-=0, no evidence) and Uncertain (small S+ with S-=0, low-confidence positive evidence); classifies contradictions into five structural types (Direct: p and not-p asserted in the same context; Source: two equal-authority provenance origins disagree; Rule: two derivation rules conflict; Observation: empirical observation contradicts a predicted/derived state; Interpretation: disagreement from conflicting ontology-mapping schemas), each with a formal triggering condition.

type_signature.codomain: boolean Contr(p), plus a Type in {Direct,Source,Rule,Observation,Interpretation}

invariants: Contr != Underdetermined != Uncertain (each with a distinct threshold condition)

assumptions.statement: a fixed threshold tau separates sufficient from insufficient evidence

rows.anchor: Non-Explosion Postulate: for all q not in ImpactScope(p), K |-_KOS q iff (K \ {p}) |-_KOS q ... Contr_scope(p) = {p} union Dependents(p) union ConflictingSources(p) ... Query Quarantine: any query Q(q) where q in Contr_scope(p) returns state CONTRADICTION_LOCAL ... Global Immunity: any query Q(r) where r not in Contr_scope(p) executes normally, completely unaffected.
rows.statement: Formalizes a non-explosion postulate for KnowledgeOS deduction: any query q outside a proposition p's ImpactScope must be answerable identically whether or not p is in the knowledge graph; defines the isolation boundary Contr_scope(p) as the union of p itself, its dependents, and its conflicting sources; requires queries inside the scope to return CONTRADICTION_LOCAL (with both branches' provenance) and queries outside the scope to execute completely unaffected (Global Immunity).

type_signature.domain: knowledge graph K and proposition p in contradiction
type_signature.codomain: the isolation set Contr_scope(p) subseteq K

invariants: queries outside Contr_scope(p) are completely unaffected by p's contradiction

rows.anchor: LifecycleState in {DETECTED, ISOLATED, TRIAGED, RESOLVED} ... Resolution Operators (delta_res): Supersede delta_super(p,P_new) Source Lineage Override ... Contextualize delta_ctx(p,C1,C2) Context Bifurcation, splits p into p(C1) and not-p(C2) ... Retract delta_retract(p,P_i) Assertion Withdrawal ... Discount delta_discount(P_i,w) Weight Discounting, applies weight penalty w in [0,1) driving support below decision threshold tau.
rows.statement: Defines a four-state contradiction lifecycle (DETECTED -> ISOLATED -> TRIAGED -> RESOLVED) and four named resolution operators with formal signatures: Supersede (deprecates old provenance in favor of a new authoritative source, zeroing the opposing support dimension), Contextualize (bifurcates a contradictory proposition into two context-scoped, no-longer-conflicting propositions), Retract (withdraws an assertion from a specific source, zeroing its support), and Discount (applies a weight penalty driving a source's support below the decision threshold) -- with a Python ContradictionEngine reference implementation performing threshold-based detection and quarantine-scope construction.

rows.statement: Rejects SPEC-CONTR's identification of Contr with the specific FDE both-positive/both-negative threshold condition as over-closure: FDE was only ever shown to be a useful representation of positive/negative support, not a complete contradiction semantics, and it still collapses important distinctions. Proposes the narrower closed claim 'Contr := detectable conflict condition' while 'Contr=(S+>0 and S->0)' with its specific threshold/evidence numeric semantics remains a candidate, not established.

rows.anchor: The non-explosion principle is strongly supported. But the exact isolation boundary {p} union Dependents(p) union ConflictingSources(p) is a specific design choice, not something we mathematically derived. Likewise 'any query outside the contradiction scope executes normally' is stronger than what was demonstrated ... Non-explosion: CLOSED principle. Exact Contr_scope algorithm: OPEN candidate. Universal global immunity theorem: OPEN.
rows.statement: Splits SPEC-CONTR's isolation claims into three separately-graded parts: non-explosion as a principle is CLOSED (strongly supported); the exact Contr_scope(p) construction ({p} union Dependents(p) union ConflictingSources(p)) is a design choice, not a derived theorem, so remains an OPEN candidate; and the universal claim that queries outside the scope always execute completely unaffected is a stronger 'global immunity theorem' than what was ever demonstrated, also OPEN.
missing: a proof of the universal global-immunity theorem, or a scoped restatement of it

rows.anchor: A new programme: three_model_convergence/. Not renamed -- properly structured artifacts (numbered per-file records, TSV control registers, a protocol, a resume script). The protocol's eight non-negotiables: 1. reading order is log order, no skipping repetitive files. 2. no premature merge -- three models reconstructed independently before comparison. 3. no circular validation: Gītā !=> Mathematics !=> Kernel !=> Gītā. 4. no hindsight bias -- read in the state of research at its date. 5. no silent promotion: hypothesis !-> definition, analogy !-> mathematics, interpretation !-> fact, probability !-> knowledge, philosophical concept !-> operator. 6. falsification is mandatory, not optional. 7. the strongest statement made must never exceed the strength of the available evidence. 8. the original corpus is READ-ONLY.
rows.statement: Discovers a newly-instantiated, properly-structured (not merely renamed) research programme, 'three_model_convergence/', which operationalizes the discipline this whole track has been discovering as an EXECUTABLE eight-non-negotiable protocol: (1) reading order is log order, no skipping; (2) no premature merge -- reconstruct all three models independently before comparing; (3) no circular validation (Gita cannot validate mathematics validating the Kernel validating Gita); (4) no hindsight bias, read documents in the research-state of their own date; (5) no silent promotion (hypothesis!->definition, analogy!->mathematics, interpretation!->fact, probability!->knowledge, philosophical concept!->operator); (6) falsification mandatory; (7) 'the strongest statement made must never exceed the strength of the available evidence' -- adopted verbatim as this programme's own governing rule; (8) the original corpus is strictly read-only.

G-99/G-106 broken intake, unschedulable programme -> a reading manifest with an explicit order. STATUS.md closes with: 'Elegance is not a qualification for canonicity.'
rows.statement: Shows the new protocol concretely operationalizes five previously-abstract registered governance findings from this batch: G-101/G-102 (parallel minting) via a read-only corpus plus a single control register; G-104 (inherited gates, partial) via an explicit guard file forbidding canonical writes until an earlier phase completes; PA-1 (no mechanism notices unperformed commissions) via a progress.tsv/resume.py system where provisional classifications are never erased and every change is logged with reason; S-Q1 (four-way status split) via an expanded 13-value classification vocabulary; and G-99/G-106 (broken intake/unschedulable programme) via an explicit ordered reading manifest -- closing with the memorable governing line 'elegance is not a qualification for canonicity.'

sources.note: Step 195's argument that identity is defined relative to a bounded context's domain model, not universally; formalizes a per-context identity equivalence relation (I_48), an identity-resolution pipeline, and the aggregate-boundary-is-not-identity DDD safeguard (I_51).

rows.anchor: Identity_{BC_1}(x) may differ from: Identity_{BC_2}(x). ... The question is not 'What is the one true identity?' The question is: 'Identity according to which domain model?'
rows.statement: Identity is context-dependent: the same real-world thing can have distinct identities in different bounded contexts (e.g. a VM in Infrastructure BC, the Nexus service in Application BC, 'Artifact Repository Service' in Business BC), connected by explicit typed relations (Represents, Hosts) rather than collapsed into one universal identity; the migration example (is Nexus_B the same system as Nexus_A?) has no universally correct answer, only a context-dependent one.

rows.anchor: x\equiv_C y means: x and y are considered the same entity under context C's identity rules. ... Reflexivity ... Symmetry ... Transitivity ... identity equivalence forms equivalence classes.
rows.statement: Defines a per-bounded-context identity equivalence relation x=_C y satisfying reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity, forming equivalence classes; a reconciliation system producing a contradictory triple (A=B, B=C, A!=C) is an identity consistency violation.

rows.anchor: I_48: Identity equivalence must be transitive within a defined identity context.
rows.statement: New invariant I_48: identity equivalence must be transitive within a defined identity context.

rows.anchor: P(x=y\mid E)=0.98 does not mean: x=y with probability 0.98 in a metaphysical sense. It is an epistemic assessment.
rows.statement: Identity reconciliation is itself an epistemic process: an identity assertion x=_C y can carry attached Evidence (migration record, certificate, registry, configuration, ownership, architectural decision), and a probabilistic identity-match score P(x=y|E) is an epistemic confidence, not a metaphysical probability of equality; some domains (e.g. passport numbers under a defined authority) support deterministic identity instead, so KnowledgeOS should support both deterministic and probabilistic identity assessment.

rows.anchor: Representation \rightarrow CandidateMatch \rightarrow Evidence \rightarrow IdentityAssessment \rightarrow IdentityDetermination. This is structurally identical to the epistemic pipeline we derived earlier.
rows.statement: Defines an identity-resolution pipeline structurally identical to the earlier general epistemic pipeline, taken as a sign of architectural coherence; an AI's identity claim ('these two repositories are the same system') should initially be a CandidateIdentityClaim requiring evidence, never an automatic silent merge.

rows.anchor: DomainEntityIdentity \neq AggregateBoundary. An entity can participate in relationships with entities outside its aggregate.
rows.statement: DDD safeguard: an aggregate root must have a domain identity and its invariants apply within that identity's boundary, but Identity does not dictate the TransactionBoundary -- an aggregate must not automatically absorb every representation of the same real-world thing, and identity does not equal aggregate boundary.

rows.anchor: I_51: Domain identity must be defined by domain semantics, not inferred solely from technical representation.
rows.statement: New broader invariant I_51: domain identity must be defined by domain semantics, never inferred solely from technical representation -- summarizing the chapter's central DDD argument.

sources.note: Peirce-derived bounded context proposal: Inquiry owns Question/investigation/hypotheses/doubt/evidence requests/acquisition/competing explanations/progress/stopping conditions/unresolved questions/research path/history, but does NOT own Knowledge; its output (InquiryResult) can be Assessment/CandidateClaim/NotProven/InsufficientEvidence/Conflict, with the Knowledge Core deciding what becomes authoritative; belief is argued to be a distinct kind from knowledge (not merely higher-confidence belief), per Prichard.

rows.anchor: Peirce describes doubt as something that stimulates inquiry, while belief establishes a disposition that guides future action. ... Inquiry is not the same thing as Knowledge.

rows.anchor: Distributed replica divergence is legitimate propagation delay, not corruption; DataConsistency != DecisionSufficiency; domain-specific consistency policy
rows.statement: States two nodes with different knowledge (node A has E1, node B has not yet received it) is not automatically corruption -- may simply reflect PropagationDelay>0. Experiment 10: temporary replica divergence yields TemporarilyDifferentViews, not Corruption -- PASS. Requires nodes to track LastUpdated/Staleness so a decision policy can judge sufficiency. Experiment 11: a safety-critical decision requiring Freshness<5min against a 20-min-stale replica is DecisionBlocked -- PASS, giving DataConsistency != DecisionSufficiency (a replica can be internally consistent yet too stale for a given decision). States consistency requirements are domain-specific (e.g. Eventual for EvidenceContext, Strong for AuthorizationContext); experiment 12: applying strong consistency to every operation is OverEngineering with unnecessary performance/availability cost -- explicitly FAIL.

experiment.hypothesis: A single universal strong-consistency policy applied to every KnowledgeOS operation is architecturally wrong; consistency requirements must be domain-specific.
experiment.setup: Experiment 12 (72.31): applying strong consistency uniformly across all operations.
experiment.assumptions: Different bounded contexts have legitimately different consistency needs (e.g. EvidenceContext eventual, AuthorizationContext strong).
experiment.method: Evaluate the cost/benefit of universal strong consistency against domain-specific requirements.
experiment.result: FAIL: OverEngineering with unnecessary performance/availability cost.
experiment.interpretation: Consistency policy must be set per bounded context, not globally.
experiment.limitations: A design-level judgment rather than a runnable benchmark.
experiment.conclusion: Experiment 12 FAIL (confirming the anti-pattern).

rows.anchor: TransactionBoundary≈InvariantBoundary heuristic (oversized-transaction FAIL); saga-like cross-context workflows with partial state
rows.statement: States a transaction should normally correspond to an invariant boundary: artifacts A,B,C connected by an invariant belong in one transaction; unconnected D,E may commit independently -- TransactionBoundary ~= InvariantBoundary ('an excellent DDD heuristic', not always exact). Experiment 13: putting the entire KnowledgeOS state into one global transaction yields PoorScalability and BoundedContextViolation -- explicitly FAIL. For cross-context workflows (Decision -> Authorization -> Execution -> Outcome) that cannot share one ACID transaction, requires WorkflowState and compensating actions (saga pattern). Experiment 14: Authorization succeeding while Execution fails correctly records AuthorizationSucceeded / ExecutionFailed as partial workflow state -- PASS, reinforcing Authorization != Execution and Decision != Outcome under distributed execution.

experiment.hypothesis: A single global ACID transaction spanning the entire KnowledgeOS state is architecturally unsound.
experiment.setup: Experiment 13 (72.34): one global transaction wrapping the whole system state.

experiment.method: Evaluate scalability and bounded-context isolation under one global transaction.

experiment.interpretation: Transaction boundaries must track invariant boundaries, never the whole system.
